1.pericope_label: O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee... because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee

schools.summary: Read the title and the verbs philologically. Ellicott derives 'early will I seek thee' from the cognate noun for dawn, so the sense is waking rather than haste, and rearranges v.2 so that the sanctuary vision is a spiritual seeing behind the outward signs. Delitzsch supplies the liturgical afterlife of the psalm.

Anchor the psalm in the Judaean flight and in covenant possession. Calvin lists the hiding-places in Judah and calls the psalm pious meditation rather than petition; Gill makes 'my God' a covenant claim independent of place, and argues that life without God's love is death.

Prefer the Hebrew text and the plain devotional sense. Clarke rules against the versions' Idumea on manuscript evidence, keeps the sanctuary vision to public ordinances, and presses the plural 'lives' to mean good beyond countless ages of human existence; Wesley reads the morning as diligence and speed.

Draw the practical lesson from the wilderness setting. Henry observes that God's dearest servants may have their lot cast in a wilderness and that prayer turns quickly into praise; Spurgeon makes David's undoubting 'my God' a rebuke to timorous professors.
Allegorise the desert. Augustine, following the Idumea reading, takes it for this world and this life of toil, and hears in the thirst a promise that whoever thirsts here will be satisfied hereafter.

debates.question: Does the title's wilderness belong to Judah or to Idumaea?

positions.view: Judah. There is 'no evidence that David had ever taken refuge in the deserts of Idumea', and all the manuscripts favour the Hebrew text.
Idumaea, as the ancient versions read it, understood allegorically: 'by the name of Idumaea is understood this world'.

debates.question: What is it to have seen God in the sanctuary?

positions.view: Something literally seen there: the ark, 'as the Jewish writers generally interpret it', or the power and glory displayed in God's public ordinances.
A vision behind the sight. The received English weakens the sense; read 'in the sanctuary have I had vision of thee in seeing thy might and glory'.

outliers.view: Alone records the psalm's liturgical afterlife, as 'the morning Psalm of the ancient church with which the singing of the Psalms was always introduced at the Sunday service'.

themes: O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is;
To see thy power and thy glory, so as I have seen thee in the sanctuary.
Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee.
Thus will I bless thee while I live: I will lift up my hands in thy name.

5.pericope_label: My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness... in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice

schools.summary: Correct the grammar and set the frame. Ellicott detaches the banquet figure from the sacrificial feasts, fixes the tense as past, notes the plural 'beds' and the three Jewish watches, and renders the last verb's double idea as 'hung upon thee'. Delitzsch marks the strophe turning towards the foes.

Read the images typically and personally. Gill argues that fat was not to be eaten under the law and so cannot be literal, takes the plural beds from David's flight from place to place, and makes the cleaving a union like that of man and wife.

Turn the verses into practice. Clarke measures spiritual satisfaction against bodily sufficiency, makes v.6 a rule of the bedside, and finds in 'my soul cleaves, or is glued, after thee' both the diligence of pursuit and the fastness of the hold; Wesley keeps the satisfaction conditional on the desire being fulfilled.

Henry sets the two readings of the wings side by side without choosing, and distinguishes within the bird image between the eagle's young, which speaks divine power, and the hen's, which speaks divine tenderness.

debates.question: Is the banquet image bound to the sacrificial feasts?

positions.view: No. The figure 'need not be connected with the sacrificial feasts' at all.
Yes, and that is the point. Fat could not be eaten under the law, so David must have meant the typical sense 'or otherwise he would speak contrary to the law of God'.
The cherubim's, stretched over the ark, so that the rejoicing is in covenant and communion.
A bird's, under which the helpless young shelter — an image made exact by the chicks running under the hen when a bird of prey appears.

outliers.view: Alone treats the verses structurally, marking the closing strophe as the turn towards the foes from whom the psalmist has retreated into the desert.

themes: My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips:
When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches.
Because thou hast been my help, therefore in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice.
My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me.

9.pericope_label: But those that seek my soul, to destroy it, shall go into the lower parts of the earth... but the king shall rejoice in God

schools.summary: Ellicott presses the Hebrew: 'they shall pour him on to the hands of the sword', the suffix collective of the enemy; the animals are jackals, not foxes; and 'sweareth by him' may be allegiance to the king or the one oath allowed an Israelite, by the name of Jehovah.

Gill bounds what the enemies could reach — the life, not the soul, 'immaterial and immortal, and could never be destroyed by man' — fixes the fulfilment on Saul and his sons with antichrist beyond, and reads the rejoicing king as David or rather the King Messiah.

Clarke gives both the burial and the infernal reading of the lower parts of the earth, offers two constructions of the jackals' portion, and holds a Davidic and an exilic sense of the king open together; Wesley takes the plainest line throughout.
Spurgeon states the retribution as a principle: destroyers destroyed, hunters made victims, the pit digged for others receiving the digger.

debates.question: Where do 'the lower parts of the earth' lead?

positions.view: To burial and the underworld of the dead — 'they shall be slain and buried in the earth, and shall be seen no more'.
To hell, 'which many supposed to be in the center of the earth', as the Old Psalter reads it.

debates.question: Who is the king that shall rejoice?

positions.view: David himself — 'I who am already anointed king', who 'shall come to the kingdom according to the promise of God'.
Rather the King Messiah, rejoicing 'because of the good of his people'.
Or, if the psalm belongs to the captivity, the royal line preserved in Zerubbabel until the Messiah come.

debates.question: By whom do the blessed swear?

positions.view: By the king, swearing allegiance — a reading that 'suits the context'.
By God, the only oath allowed the Israelite, binding themselves by his authority and devoting themselves to his service.

outliers.view: The only voice to separate what the enemies could destroy from what they could not, exempting the soul from their reach altogether.

themes: But those that seek my soul, to destroy it, shall go into the lower parts of the earth.
They shall fall by the sword: they shall be a portion for foxes.
But the king shall rejoice in God; every one that sweareth by him shall glory: but the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped.
